lessons.title: Feeding and grazing management
lessons.html:
Feeding and grazing management

Feed is the biggest single cost and the biggest driver of production on a livestock farm. On extensive farms, the cheapest feed is well-managed veld.

Carrying capacity and stocking rate

Carrying capacity is how many hectares one large stock unit needs to graze sustainably. It is set by rainfall, veld type and veld condition. The stocking rate is how many animals are actually on the land. When the stocking rate is higher than the carrying capacity, the veld degrades and animals lose condition. Your farm manager or local extension officer can tell you the guideline for your area.

Rotational grazing

Moving animals through camps gives grazed plants time to recover. Watch grass height and move animals before the best grasses are grazed to the ground. Keep records of which camp was grazed when.

Sweetveld and sourveld

Sweetveld keeps its feed value in winter. Sourveld grows well in summer but loses protein in winter, so animals on sourveld need a protein lick in the dry season.

Supplementation

  • Summer: phosphate lick, because many South African soils are low in phosphorus.
  • Winter: protein (and often energy) lick so rumen microbes can digest dry grass.
  • Production lick: for animals that must grow fast or produce milk.

Always follow the feed supplier's label for intake and never give urea-containing licks to hungry animals without the correct introduction, because urea poisoning can kill.

Water

Water is the most important nutrient. Check troughs, windmills, solar pumps and reservoirs on every round. Animals without water lose production within hours and can die within days in summer.

lessons.title: Breeding management
lessons.html:
Breeding management

Seasonal breeding

Most extensive farms use a short, fixed breeding season so that calves or lambs are born when the veld is at its best and weaning happens before winter. A short season gives a uniform group of young animals that is easier to manage and sell. Bulls are typically put with cows for a limited number of weeks, and then removed.

Selecting breeding animals

  • Choose females that conceive every year, rear their young well and have sound udders, feet and teeth.
  • Cull females that skip a year, have bad udders or poor mothering.
  • Buy bulls and rams from reputable breeders with performance records and a breeding soundness test.
  • Keep a ratio of males to females suitable for the camp size and terrain; ask your manager for the farm's target.

Pregnancy testing

A vet can test cows for pregnancy a few weeks after the bulls are removed. Open (empty) cows can then be sold or managed separately rather than eating feed for a year without producing.

Calving and lambing season

Move heavily pregnant females to camps near the homestead with shelter and good access. Check them often. Record each birth: date, dam tag, sex, birth weight if possible. Ensure every newborn drinks colostrum. Protect lambs from jackals and caracal with kraaling, guard dogs or alpacas, or shepherding.

Key measures

MeasureWhat it tells you
Conception rateHow many females got pregnant
Weaning percentageYoung weaned per 100 females mated
Weaning weightMothering ability and veld quality
MortalityLosses from disease, predators, weather

lessons.title: Handling, marking and marketing
lessons.html:
Handling, marking and marketing

Low-stress handling

Animals that are handled calmly gain more weight, get injured less and are safer to work with. Work with the animal's flight zone: stand at the edge of it to move animals forward, and use the point of balance at the shoulder. Do not shout, hit or use dogs in the crush. Well-designed kraals, races and crushes with solid sides help. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty an offence.

Safety when handling

  • Never stand directly behind a cow or horse, or in a crush with an animal.
  • Watch bulls, cows with new calves and rams closely - they can charge.
  • Always know your escape route in a kraal.
  • Use the head clamp and neck bar correctly; keep fingers out of gates.

Identification and routine procedures

Animals must be identified, for example by ear tag, tattoo or brand. Marks used for ownership must be registered under the Animal Identification Act. Routine procedures include castration, dehorning, tail docking in lambs and hoof trimming. These must be done at the right age, with the right equipment and, where required, pain relief and supervision by a vet. Keep instruments clean and treat wounds against flies.

Weaning and marketing

Weaning separates young from their mothers so that females regain condition. Weigh young animals at weaning and select replacements. Sell surplus animals at auctions, to feedlots or directly to abattoirs. Animals should be in good condition, correctly identified and moved with the required documents. Transport them so they can stand, with no overcrowding, and with water before and after long trips.

Key points

  • Keep the stocking rate within the veld's carrying capacity.
  • Supplement phosphate in summer and protein in winter.
  • A short breeding season gives uniform young and easier management.
  • Handle animals calmly and always keep an escape route.
  • Record births, weights, treatments and sales.

quiz.question: What happens when the stocking rate is higher than the carrying capacity?

options.text: The veld degrades and animals lose condition
